newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian reformers sweep into government.
newsitem.headline: Russian reformers sweep into government.

text.p: Liberal reformers were set to take a firm grip on Russia's new government after Boris Yeltsin surprisingly handed a top job to a young regional chief on Monday and several other liberals were brought in or promoted.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said his new government, spearheaded by first deputy premiers Anatoly Chubais, 41, and Boris Nemtsov, 37-year-old governor of Nizhny Novgorod region, would include several fellow reformers at deputy premier level.
Keeping a promise to press ahead with stalled free market reforms, Soviet-style industrial management minstries, including the Industry Ministry, would be scrapped or downgraded.

Deputy Economy Minister Yakov Urinson will step up to become Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister. He is likely to report to Chubais, former privatisation supremo and Kremlin chief-of-staff, who will have overall charge of economic reform and was reported to be taking the finance ministry for himself.

Alfred Kokh, head of the State Property Committee and so effectively Russia's privatisation minister, was also promoted to Deputy Prime Minister. Reformist communications minister Vladimir Bulgak will be deputy premier overseeing technology.
The more conservative Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov stays on as deputy prime minister as does Valery Serov, who is in charge of dealing with other former Soviet republics.
The rest of the cabinet line-up would be announced by the end of the week, Chernomyrdin said in televised remarks.

The liberal mayor of the industrial city of Samara will join the cabinet at the same rank, Chernomyrdin said, stressing that the Moscow leadership was turning its attention to the problems of Russia's regions. Millions of workers and pensioners have not been paid and labour unions plan a day of protests on March 27.
Also with profound regional experience, Nemtsov was a surprise appointment since Yeltsin had said Chubais would be Chernomyrdin's only first deputy.

Nemtsov, whose boyish good looks and sharp mind have already earned Yeltsin's praise as a potential successor, was seen by some analysts as having been brought in to build a bridge between Chubais and the more conservative Chernomyrdin, 58.
"There is a very interesting variant," Yeltsin was shown on television as telling a slightly concerned-looking Nemtsov.

"Two young men -- you and Anatoly Chubais -- create a fresh young team in the government -- from scratch. No one else has been appointed yet. All candidates to the government would be agreed with the two first deputy premiers."
Russian liberals, who have criticised Yeltsin for a lack of progress in market reforms, hailed Nemtsov's appointment as a sign the president was committed to the reformist course.
"This is a movement in the right direction," RIA news agency quoted Viktor Sheinis of the liberal Yabloko party as saying.

Yeltsin, worried by the growing tension caused by chronic delays in wages and pensions and the government's inability to handle the crisis, has told Chernomyrdin to review the structure of the cabinet and dramatically improve its performance.
Yeltsin said that Nemtsov would handle social programmes, natural monopolies and deal with powerful regional authorities.
Nemstov himself said he would take on monopolies. Many big industrialists see Chernomyrdin, a former gas industry chief, as a defender of their interests.
By stepping in to the delicate issue of forming the cabinet, Yeltsin also reminded the other players that he held the top authority and that months of illness were definitely over.

"I am in good form today. Today I am able, so to say, to rule the state and in fact in better form today than before the illness and I will of course rule Russia up to new elections in 2000," he said in an interview shown on Russian Television.
Political analysts say that Nemtsov's new job was crucial for the success of the cabinet. But they add that dealing with such sensitive issues could prove politically fatal for him.

Yeltsin broke the stalemate in the government reshuffle days before heading off to Helsinki for a summit with President Bill Clinton on Thursday and Friday. U.S. and Russian officials have been trying to hammer out a deal that the two men could announce to ease tensions over NATO's expansion plans.

Yeltsin made clear on Monday that Russia's patience was not endless. "I don't want a return to the Cold War, I don't want it and our people don't want it, but for that there must be equal conditions in the world order," he said.
